The pun landed.
The reason to switch didn’t.

Klaviyo’s ad wins a smile with a banana pun, “a more a-peeling CRM.” But it never says why a brand should actually switch, no proof, no numbers, and the page doesn’t close the gap either.

What the roast found · tap to open each one

What’s happening

The banana peel plus “ripe for an upgrade” lands the metaphor and earns attention on a crowded feed.

The fix

Keep the pun, it works. Just make it carry a reason, not only a smile.

What’s happening

“A more a-peeling CRM” is all style. It names no retention lift, no revenue number, no capability a brand would move platforms for.

The fix

Name one concrete win: a retention lift, a revenue figure, or a specific thing Klaviyo does that the current tool can’t.

What’s happening

There’s no customer name, stat, or logo, so a marketer who’d have to justify a migration has nothing to point to.

The fix

Add a named customer and a number, a skeptical buyer won’t switch on wordplay.

What’s happening

“Switch to Klaviyo” is a brand line, not an action. The ad looks like an offer but never tells you what happens next.

The fix

Swap the brand line for a real next step tied to a specific offer.

What’s happening

The click lands on the broad brand page, so the “why switch” the ad skipped never gets answered after the click either.

The fix

Open the page with the proof and the specific win the ad should have promised.

Why it scores 6/10 · tap a row

The pun works once you get the banana, but it delays the actual message by a beat on a cold feed.
The banana peel plus “ripe for an upgrade” is a tight, memorable pun that lands the metaphor instead of just decorating it.
No real CTA beyond “Switch to Klaviyo,” a brand statement, not an action. It looks like an offer but never asks for the click.
Zero specifics: no retention lift, no unified data, no channels. It’s style with no substance behind it.
No customer names, numbers, or proof anywhere, just the wordplay and a logo.

Questions, answered

The creative is memorable and the pun lands. The gap is substance: there’s no proof, no number, and no specific reason to switch, so a skeptical marketer has nothing concrete to act on.
Attention isn’t the problem, it earns the smile. The problem is the next beat: nothing tells the buyer why to switch, and the page doesn’t fill that in, so the click doesn’t compound into pipeline.
Read your ad and ask: after the laugh, what’s the reason to act, and is it on the page? If the only thing carrying the click is tone, that’s the gap. AdRoast scores this automatically from your website. The first roast is free.
